en: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Sulāta.
Translated at the Baima Monastery in Luoyang by the Śramaṇa Baiyan of the Western Regions during the Cao Wei period.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with...
There was a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, together with five thousand bodhisattvas.

At that time, in the city of Śrāvastī, there was an extremely poor man named Sudatta (Sūrata), whose firm resolve was unshakable. He placed his faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, taking refuge in the Triple Gem; he upheld the pure precepts and practiced the ten wholesome deeds. Possessing the four immeasurable minds, he rescued and aided others without weariness; his inner nature was pure, and his realization of self and bliss was non-dual. With sincere intent, he sought the unsurpassed Great Way of the Buddha, contemplating his practice and reciting it day and night. Through skillful means, he guided and benefited all people, remaining content in poverty and finding joy in the Dharma.

Thereupon, Śakra, Lord of Devas, beheld with his divine eye the extraordinary excellence of Sūrata’s merit: he was undeluded by what he heard and had widely studied the various sūtras; he was free from deviant conduct, remaining composed and dignified in sitting and rising; in walking, stopping, lying down, or waking, he never failed in proper decorum; he had few desires and was easily satisfied, not coveting gain or offerings; he was upright and spoke well, his words being trustworthy and devoid of ornamentation; he observed the fasts and precepts with frugality, tempering his food and clothing; using leaves for vessels and grass for mats, he kept no livestock and eliminated all possessions, storing nothing away; thus, neither kings nor commoners failed to revere and love him.

He constantly visited the Buddha three times each day and three times each night to inquire about and receive the teachings with faith; knowing his intention, the Buddha would always grant him an audience.

Whenever Sulabha went to see the Buddha, hundreds of countless people would invariably accompany him, and wherever he traveled, stayed, slept, arose, or practiced walking meditation, devas and humans protected him.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, thought to himself:
"This benevolent one is fully perfected in his ethical conduct; I fear my own position will be usurped by him.
I shall now test him to ascertain which path he truly seeks."
Śakra then manifested as several men who kicked and reviled Sūrata without restraint.
They further hurled stones at him and struck him with staffs; yet, through the power of his forbearance and his compassionate benevolence, Sūrata felt neither anger nor resentment.
Śakra then manifested as several people and said to Sūrata, "I am truly here before you;
what do you think of my killing you? Sūrata replied:
"What you have plotted is not a wholesome dharma.
Even if someone were to cut my body with a blade, I would still harbor no resentment; how much less so for mere beating and abuse? Why is this so? [Because...]"
Now, there are two kinds of fruits for transgressions and blessings:
those who plant blessings are born in the heavens, while those who commit transgressions fall into the evil realms.
Therefore, one should not harbor resentment, much less desire to harm others.
Thereupon, Sūrata spoke these verses:
"By planting the seeds of evil, One is thus born into the class of those who fall into sin;
If one plants the roots of goodness, One will surely expect the fruit of merit hereafter."
Awaken to evil through contemplation; one should maintain wisdom to discern it.
Evil is not the root of goodness; by planting virtue, there will be no evil fruit.
By guarding the three [doors], one can be free from evil; let body, speech, and mind always be good.
The superior person endures without resentment; the wise accept [adversity] without transgression.
By eliminating the three [defilements], one becomes pure;
when body, speech, and mind are without flaw, those who are encouraged to practice merit will surely attain their wishes and abide in constant peace.
The emanated person could not cause the country to become poor, nor did Sūrata harbor even the slightest malicious intent; thereupon, the emanated person withdrew.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again placed gold and silver before him and had the emanated person say to Sūrata:
"Virtuous one, take these treasures and use them as you please to practice generosity and create merit, or enjoy fine clothing and delicious food; how can poverty be endured?"
Sudra said: "According to my past deeds, I ought to undergo this poverty and suffering; because I greedily and falsely seized treasures, my future distress will surely be even more severe."
The manifested person said, "Enjoy yourself and take pleasure for the rest of your life;
how could you know what will happen hereafter? Sudāna replied:
"This is not the speech of wisdom.
To lack foresight regarding one's own person and subsequently incur great suffering is what the wise fear;
to covet vast stores and seize what does not belong to oneself, with a sin equal to that of theft, is what the wise despise."

Out of attachment to the body and the calculation for longevity, one seeks self-preservation and avoids death; yet such a person commits the offense of taking what is not given, which the wise do not do.

Indeed, the wise calculate that the body and life are impermanent and that all things are not "mine"; since they value only the Way, they are free from greed and contention, and simply maintain goodness.
Furthermore, he spoke in verse:
"Though one may store treasures amounting to a thousand billion, if they are not given away, one will regret them at the time of death.
The wise call such a person poor; one should recognize these words as ultimate truth."
Moderating one's diet and not clinging to flavors, being sincere and truthful while delighting in giving,
and possessing wisdom and reflection as one’s wealth— the Buddha says this is constant peace.
Being able to refrain from doing evil and guarding the Way so that both within and without are pure— this is true tranquility.
To be self-adorned without precepts, having already committed such transgressions, is not the mark of a worthy one.
One should receive instruction from a wise teacher; do not rely on the praise of the foolish.
The praise of fools drags one into darkness, while a wise teacher brings one closer to purity.
The manifested person was unable to arouse any thoughts of greed in Sūrata, so he withdrew.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, manifested again, carrying pearls worth several hundred million, and approached Sūrata, saying:
"I have been engaged in a legal dispute with another man, and the matter has reached the King."
"I venture to cite you, a man of benevolence, as my witness; I wish to offer this jewel to you, hoping you will kindly provide a word of testimony.
Sūrata replied, "Why should I say such a thing?"
This is what I fear, and I shall never dare to deceive. Why is this?
One who speaks falsely first deceives themselves, then deceives Heaven, and also deceives the Dharma.
It causes one’s breath to be foul, one’s words to go unheeded, and one to be frequently slandered; the mind remains perpetually withered.

Disregarded by the heavens, the complexion of the body changes, merit and fortune wane, and a good reputation is lost. Such a person is tormented and deceived by the sages and worthies of past ages; having lost the root of virtue and giving rise to manifold evils, they block the path to goodness and cast themselves into the darkness of error, thereby inviting calamity and guilt in future lives.
He further spoke in verse:
"Deceiving the multitude brings forth evil fruits, Causing one's own mouth to be perpetually foul-smelling;
Having completely forgotten previous words, One enters into error, where the right path is lost."
To deceive oneself is also to deceive Heaven; to deceive the Dharma is to bring sorrow upon oneself.
One will constantly be suspected by the multitude; what benefit does such deceit bring to others?
Deceit is the root of all evils, severing one’s own connection to wholesome deeds.
Therefore, this leads to a mass of suffering; what benefit is there for a person in false speech?

Even if one were to bestow upon them gold, silver, and pearls sufficient to fill the world, when it comes to those who uphold the laws and precepts, when would they ever be deceived by such treasures?
The emanated being was unable to cause Sūrata to speak falsely, and immediately withdrew.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, returned and said to his wife:
"Take my courtesans and go together with several women of the Pañcāla clan; visit Sūrata and try to change his mind, corrupting his pure conduct. See whether he has lust or not."
The Heavenly Queen accepted the instruction and, accompanied by her handmaidens, arrived at the dwelling of Susīla during the quiet hours of the night.
From the midst of the sky, she spoke in exquisite and elegant words:
"Virtuous One, please arise; the gods have sent us to attend upon you."

Our forms and features are handsome, our garments are bright and fresh, and we are adorned with necklaces, jewels, robes, and sandalwood incense. Being neither too old nor too young, we are perfectly suited to this time; our appearance is upright, pure, and radiant, such that one cannot help but gaze upon us. It is by virtue of your merit that we have come to serve you.

Sudra looked up and replied, "All of you are beloved by those in the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts; you are not what those of superior wisdom among devas and humans delight in."
I see all that you possess as being like dream-images of forms and fragrances; in reality, they are like bubbles upon the ocean.

I see your physical forms as mere skeletons smeared with flesh and drenched in blood, bound by sinews and enveloped in skin and hide to conceal the filth and stains—just like the eyes and ears of a conjured man created by a master illusionist.

When you all ascend, I shall witness impermanence; you shall undergo decay and become subject to the law of separation. I have already awakened to both demerit and merit, and I harbor not even a hair’s breadth of affectionate attachment.
You truly destroy the wholesome minds of others and are unable to establish the intentions of people;

you do nothing but defile pure conduct. You are thus linked with stench and decay; addicted to desire without finding joy, you bring about suffering for yourselves. By your own error, you fall into darkness and enter the three evil paths. Desire is not the root of goodness; strife, litigation, fear, and anger—the perversions, turbidity, and chaos—all arise from desire. Through folly and madness, you invite calamity and sit amidst physical deformity because of it.

Externally indulging while internally burning with feverish passion, one fails to see the fruits of merit. Because the person’s original nature belongs to the class of animals, they will subsequently become oxen, horses, mules, donkeys, camels, dogs, pigs, chickens, or geese—all brought about by desire. Having distanced themselves from the sages and worthies, they have lost faith, precepts, learning, generosity, and the path of wisdom. Following a single thought of desire without regard for future lives, this desire constantly destroys the intent to seek the Way; how much more so the rest?
Then he spoke in verse:
"To seek defilement is to become foul and putrid; To suffer alone is to distance oneself from peace and joy.
Casting oneself into the sins of the hungry ghosts, One harbors no concern while constantly associating with evil."
Lack of restraint is the root of disorder; distancing oneself from the Dharma leads to error.
Failing to consider this results in inversion; when desire flourishes, delusion increases further.
Through greed and hatred, one loses the virtuous mind; with perverse thoughts, one is constantly terrified.
Internal anxieties are like external boils; sitting idly, one wishes to destroy the root of faith.
Having already become the foundation of unwholesomeness, it is like the *pūtanā* demon devouring human liver.
Dwelling in decline while serving heterodox deities, one’s pursuit of desire is like that of a madman.
Through lust one becomes an ox, a sheep, a pig, A donkey, a horse, an elephant, or a camel;
Long enduring the suffering of animal forms, Therefore, the wise abandon desire.
Discarding faith, precepts, learning, and virtue, One casts oneself far into the evil realms.
For those who are lustful and caught in the net of delusion, it is better to distance themselves from women and always strive for swift liberation.
Even if people like you, with your handsome forms,
were to fill this Jambudvīpa and remain as steadfast in mind as mountains, how could even a celestial deity cause them to waver?

At that time, the Queen of Heaven and her handmaidens were unable to arouse any lustful thoughts in the poor Sudāna; they immediately returned to the celestial palace and spoke these verses to Śakra, the Lord of Devas:
"The son has studied deeply and perceived the Truth; He speaks of knowing the wickedness of women’s ways.
Having already abandoned form and being free from desire, He is without wounds and thus cannot receive the poison."

Thereupon, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, became even more terrified, his hair standing on end as he thought: "This benevolent one is pure in his precepts and not perverse; he will surely seize my abode. He then descended in person to visit Sūrata and spoke in verse, asking:
"What does Sūrata seek to obtain, That you are so vigorous in your pure precepts?"
"I pray you tell me: is it a king, the sun, the moon, Śakra, or Brahmā?
Thereupon, Sūrata replied to Śakra in verse:
"Though kings, the sun, the moon, the gods, Śakra, and Brahmā are indeed honored, [none are equal to the Buddha]."
All that is impermanent is like an illusion; how can one who has not yet escaped it find clarity?
May the desire for pleasure not arise, and may the afflictions of old age and death cease.
May the limits of hatred, love, enmity, and suffering be transcended, and may all beings within the three realms be delivered.
The Lord of Devas, his mind liberated and filled with joyful delight, immediately spoke this verse in praise of Sūrata:
“Excellent! Out of compassion for the world, You have swiftly attained your wish.
You shall surely eliminate the defilements of the three periods of time; Gods and humans will certainly receive your grace.”

Thereupon, as Śūradatta was walking for exercise through the city of Śrāvastī, he found a treasure from a previous kalpa in the marketplace that was worth the entire world. Taking it in his hand, he raised his voice and said:
"In this kingdom of Śrāvastī, there is one who is extremely poor; I shall bestow this treasure upon him."

At that time, there was an elder in the kingdom who had formerly been a wealthy merchant; together with several thousand others, they all rushed before Sudhana according to their karmic conditions and each spoke, saying:
"We are impoverished and destitute; we pray only for your compassion and aid."
Furthermore, there were countless people who were extremely poor, all of whom rushed forward to beg for treasures.
Sudāna replied, "Worthy ones, you are not poor.
At present, there is one in this city who is the most impoverished; I shall take these treasures and go to give them to him."
The crowd asked,
"In this city, who is the most impoverished? Sudāna replied:
"King Prasenajit is the poorest in the kingdom," they said.
The people replied, "Do not speak such words!
How could a sovereign ever be poor? Consider the treasures and rare jewels stored within his palace—they are beyond calculation."
Sudra replied to the assembly in verse:
"Though one amasses great wealth and treasures, the desire for more knows no satiety;
like water flowing day and night, such people remain as poor as ever."
"Those whose greed increases and who do not reflect upon suffering, whose minds feel no shame for their wrong conduct—
passing from this world to the next, they are the truly impoverished. Thereupon, Sūrata,
together with the great multitude of people, arrived at the gate of the royal palace.

At that time, King Prasenajit was in the main hall; he had just detained more than five hundred elders, all of whom were guilty of offenses, and the king intended to have them pay a large amount of wealth and treasures as ransom for their crimes.
An attendant informed the king that Sūrata was outside, whereupon the king invited him to have an audience.
Sūrata entered and said to the king:

"The other day, while I was walking through the city of Śrāvastī, I obtained this bright moon-jewel and intended to give it to those who are poor. Upon observing this kingdom, I found no one more destitute than Your Majesty; I pray that the Great King will accept this treasure."
Upon hearing these words, the king felt ashamed and replied,
"Sūrata! My poverty is as great as yours."
Sudāna said, "The King is poorer than I am.
The King replied:
"Please explain its meaning.
Su-lai, before the great assembly, spoke these verses for the king:
"One who greedily pursues wealth day and night without satiety Will bring harm upon himself as a ruler and suffer burning pain hereafter."
To preserve oneself from death is not merely for the sake of the future; this is called being utterly destitute and unable to practice the Dharma.

To always possess a compassionate heart without indolence, to distance oneself from sensual forms and draw near to the virtuous while knowing contentment, and to take no pleasure in seeking much or accumulating wealth—this is to live as a wise person free from resentment and malice.

Holding office, they abandon what is right to do what is wrong; using wealth to intimidate the people and inflicting punishments and laws, they remain complacent in security while forgetting danger, indulging their desires until, deceived by others and facing death in distress, it is too late for regret.
Those whose direct faith and pure consciousness are strong, Whose discipline is like knowing when to stop and who do not forget what they have heard,
Who always know and are without fear, finding joy in practice— These are called "not poor," as praised by the Sages.
One who, having attained wealth and honor, does not think of giving; who believes that life is permanent yet is ruined in this very moment;
who is greedy, corrupt, and deluded like an elephant in rut; whose mind is blocked and lacks awareness—this is what is called poverty.
Faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, and reverence for all practices; Forgiving oneself and bringing peace to others through skillful instruction;
Being neither foolish, nor angry, nor indulgent; Governing oneself by means of the Dharma—this is to be eternally wealthy.
Fire burns through grass and wood yet knows no satisfaction; The myriad streams flow into the sea yet never reach a point of fullness.
The sun and moon do not grow weary as they illuminate the four quarters; So too, greed persists until old age and death, never tiring of desire.
Though fire burns with intense heat, it does not blaze for long; wealth and honor are impermanent like floating clouds.
Therefore, wisdom does not desire heaven or kingship; the mind of wisdom burns away evil so that no smoke remains.
King Prasenajit said to Sūrata,
"Who can testify that I am poor while you are rich?
Sūrata replied:

"Great King, you have also heard that there exists in the world a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader, a trainer of persons, a teacher of gods and humans, called Buddha, the World-Honored One—one who has seen the truth for himself and is able to realize the essential through direct experience."
"Now he is not far away; he is nearby at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The king said, "I have already received a generous stipend for having been able to see this Honored One."
Sudāsa said, "This holy teacher can serve as witness.
The king said:
“I pray that the Buddha will come; whatever the Buddha has severed shall be taken as the truth.
Thereupon, Sūrata spoke these verses:
“The Buddha’s wisdom perceives all things completely; There is no need for the Great King to invite him.”
Now, according to what my mind contemplates, having seen [this], you will surely come out of compassion.
You are a sage with supernormal powers and free from outflows; as one who acts for the world’s future benefit, the Buddha possesses no uncertain knowledge.
He will surely come as King—do not doubt it.
Always free from hatred or love, he takes pity on humans and non-humans alike;
though far away in other lands, he dwells only upon his Dharma words.
I pray that Your Majesty will believe that the Buddha is the Lord of Compassion.
Thereupon, with focused mindfulness, [he thought]: "The Hero of the World will arrive before long;
I shall beforehand prepare fragrant flowers and jewels, pearl necklaces, silken canopies, and banners.
With various musicians tuning the five notes, I shall make offerings to the Buddha that are fresh and brilliant."
Sudra then joined his palms, bared his right shoulder, knelt with both knees on the ground, and from afar addressed the Buddha in verse:
“The Buddha fully knows the minds of men And perceives the sincerity of all.
I pray that you grant audience to my earnest intent And manifest your divine power before me.”
Thereupon the earth shook violently, and the Buddha, together with five hundred bhikṣus and two hundred bodhisattvas, miraculously emerged from within the earth and ascended the royal palace hall.
Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and countless hundreds of thousands of devas all followed the Buddha there.

When the king, the officials, and the common people saw the Buddha manifest his supernatural powers, there was none who was not struck with awe; they increased their reverence and prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet.
Several thousand people, out of this reverence, gave rise to the aspiration to become bodhisattvas.
Thereupon, the poor man Sudāna came forward, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand aside, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“While walking through this city, I obtained a bright moon-like golden pearl worth an entire Jambudvīpa; I thought I would give it to the poor.”
Upon examining this kingdom, the King alone is utterly impoverished. Why is this so?
Because his greed knows no satiety;

he imposes taxes without ceasing and oppresses the people without rest. The entire populace is exhausted by forced labor and coerced service; those who are upright are slandered and harmed, while the subordinates suffer from turmoil and unrest.

The one above is bound by desire; he does not contemplate impermanence nor accord with the correct governance. For this reason, when I offered him this bright moon pearl, he was unwilling to accept it and instead questioned me regarding the evidence of poverty and wealth.

"Therefore, I pray to behold the Tathāgata, who there is none whom he does not guide and none whom he does not protect. May you analyze my doubts and remove my defilements, so that I may understand this meaning.
The Buddha said, "How magnificent!"
"Śūradatta!
My words are most sincere; let not the Great King harbor any doubt.
The King said:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
May you enlighten our ignorance with words that are correct and true.
The Buddha, through his skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), protected the king’s intention and manifested these words of meaning:
“O King, listen attentively!

There are indeed causes and conditions by which one might consider Your Majesty wealthy while Sūrata has nothing; yet there is also a profound principle by which one might consider Sūrata wealthy such that Your Majesty cannot equal him.”
What is called the wealth of a king refers to the calculation of his national treasures:

gold, silver, jade, crystal, lapis lazuli, pearls, coral, mother-of-pearl, agate, elephants, horses, and palaces—all of which he possesses in abundance and governs with sovereign ease. Such royal wealth, Sūrata, does not exist for you.

One should consider that Sudāsa’s wealth consists of the correct characteristics of virtue and the Path: his generosity, observance of the precepts, power of patience, diligence, wisdom, heedfulness, and orderly conduct; his compassion, kindness, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; his love and reverence for the Triple Gem; his study of the profound, his pure intention, his straightforward faith, and his sense of shame and dread of blame; and his full possession of the seven riches. This is the wealth of Sudāsa, which no king can equal.

Even if all the people within the territories under Your Majesty’s rule were as wealthy as Śreṣṭhī Mahānāman, and one were to combine their persons and riches to compare them with the wealth of virtue possessed by Sudāsa, they would not approach even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or a hundred-millionth part; it is impossible to compare them through any analogy.
The king said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"As the World-Honored One has said, 'I am already possessed of merit, for within my realm there is a person who upholds the Dharma and is most wealthy.
The Buddha said, "Indeed,
there are also many *tathāgatas* within the king's realm."
At that time, King Prasenajit rose and stood before the Buddha, praising Sūrata, saying:
“I revere you, O benevolent one, as I do the Buddha; Because of you, I am made magnificent.
I wish to offer the position of state minister to you; From this day forth, may you be my teacher.”
For a long time I have been arrogant regarding my precepts, and dwelling in this kingdom, I have remained far from the True Dharma.
Now that I have heard the words of Sūrata, I vow to cultivate the holy life with meticulous care.
Because of greed for wealth and profit, I was imprisoned by five hundred men as an enemy.
"Now, to pardon greed would be of no benefit; rather, one should cherish benevolence, for its grace is difficult to forget.

Thereupon, the five hundred prisoners, hearing that the king had pardoned their crimes, all recollected the kindness of Sūrata. Loathing the suffering of impermanence, they attained a mind free from desire, rose together to pay homage to the Buddha, and also paid homage to Sūrata.
The king’s heart was filled with joy, and he praised him again, saying:
“You are wealthy while I am truly poor; Sūrata’s words are sublime and true.
From this day forth, I issue a decree throughout the kingdom that no one shall say you are poor.”
After the people of the country heard the king’s command, they all referred to Sūrata as "the wealthy," and the name "poor" was no longer used for him.
Sūrata rose, adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Now this great assembly has gathered."
Excellent,
World-Honored One!
We pray that you will preach the Dharma, so that these people may not have seen the Buddha in vain.
The Buddha said: "Excellent!
Listen to what I shall say and reflect upon it well."
There are four dharmas, son of good family!
by which one sees the Buddha.
What are the four?
"To have faith, to have joy, to have gladness, and to have reverence—these are the four.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas by which one may see the Buddha.
What are these four?"
Having beheld the physical form of the Buddha, they immediately give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment, vowing that in future lives they may obtain a body such as his;
having reached the stage of mental recollection, they remember the Buddha’s words as being always sincere;
and having brought forth compassion for all beings, their minds are no longer moved by worldly concerns.
Having taken delight in what one practices, one does not sever the Three Jewels; this is the fourth.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that constitute the awakening mind (bodhyanga).
What are the four?

That is to say: form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; there is nothing to behold, what is seen is transformed into emptiness, and that which is conceived is immediately known—these are the four.
"Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one sees the Buddha as pure."
What are the four?

Not reckoning self and other as internal or external is the removal [of attachment]; not reckoning permanence is the removal of the lifespan; not reckoning annihilation is the relinquishing of habitual practice; and seeing with the Buddha-eye to awaken the ever-sleeping mind—these are the four.
“Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one sees the Buddha facing purity.

What are the four? [They are: all dharmas are without this grasping; taking right concentration as pure conduct; having already trained to achieve unsurpassed wisdom; and seeing pure liberation through skillful means. These are the four.”
"Noble sons and noble daughters!
Having seen the Tathāgata, you are now oriented toward purity.

When the Buddha spoke these words, seven hundred bhikṣus attained the realization of the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*), and all the bodhisattvas present attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); thousands of people established the foundations of merit.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, he rose from his seat and, together with his disciples and bodhisattvas, manifested miraculous powers to fly away like the king of phoenixes, returning to the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Thereupon, King Prasenajit said to Sūrata,
"When you, O virtuous one, wish to go to the Buddha, I pray that you will inform me so that I may follow you.
Sūrata replied:

"I also pray that Your Majesty will command the ladies of the harem, the princes and their attendants, as well as the officials and citizens of the kingdom, that none of them shall fail to go to the Buddha; let the authorities record the offenses of those who do not."

"Why is this? It is because a bodhisattva does not merely concern himself with his own body or with humans and non-humans; rather, when a bodhisattva is in the midst of a great assembly, his majestic spiritual power is doubly magnificent.
The king said:
"I wish to hear how a bodhisattva leads a great multitude;
what should be done? Sudāna replied:

"A bodhisattva can assemble all sentient beings to serve as his followers. This means that by means of giving, he causes the multitude to follow him gladly, and he is able to transform those who are stingy so that they come to love giving."
When a bodhisattva maintains the precepts, all people joyfully follow them; they transform those who lack faith, causing them to believe in the retribution of sin and merit.
When a bodhisattva practices patience, all people joyfully follow them; they transform those who harbor anger, causing them to be free from resentment and hatred.
When a bodhisattva practices diligence, all people joyfully follow; he transforms those who lack power, causing them to establish diligence.
When a bodhisattva practices dhyāna, all people joyfully follow; he transforms those with distracted minds, causing them to maintain single-mindedness.
The wisdom of the Bodhisattva is such that all people joyfully follow it; he transforms those who are ignorant and deluded, enabling them to attain correct wisdom.
The compassion practiced by the Bodhisattva is such that all people joyfully follow it; he transforms those who lack benevolence, causing them to possess a compassionate heart.
When a bodhisattva practices compassion, the multitude joyfully follows; entering the suffering of birth and death, they do not weary of correct practice.
When a bodhisattva practices sympathetic joy, the multitude joyfully follows; transforming those who are sorrowful and deluded, they are able to cause them to delight in the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva’s conduct protects all people so that they joyfully follow him; he comforts and encourages them, leading them to enter the Dharma.
Thus it is, Great King:
his virtuous deeds are manifold.
"Furthermore, there are four matters for being a good recipient:
first, protecting sentient beings so as not to abandon them;
second, maintaining the purity of the fundamental practices of all virtues."
The third is to select excellent vows so that the Buddha-land is free from the three poisons;
the fourth is to dwell in emptiness, being without aspiration or conceptual thought, thereby escaping the constraints of all demonic nets.

The Bodhisattva constantly practices gentleness, transforming those who are stubborn and strong-willed without forgetting the Mahāyāna; he delights in dwelling among mountains and marshes, yet does not destroy or sever the merits of previous lives; as his roots of goodness increase daily, he universally cultivates all practices, fulfilling the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment that constitute the Way.
"The Bodhisattva gathers the people together by means of this.
King Prasenajit was filled with great joy and a virtuous mind arose within him; the king took off the colorful robe he was wearing, which was worth more than ten million, and gave it to Sūrata.
Sudāsa would not accept it, saying,
"If the Great King’s intention is one of joy, how does this differ from giving me the gift?
The King’s heart was displeased.
Sudāsa spoke again:
"I already possess fine garments that I wear with great pleasure; why should I use these? What need have I for these worn-out clothes?
The king said: [Continue as per source].
"Why? Śūradatta replied, "There were times when I would take off my clothes, hang them on a tree, and leave them;
for one day or even up to seven days, no one would come to take them. Yet I had no sense of attachment, nor did I look back with longing for those garments."
"A Bodhisattva always wears garments such as these; having no attachment himself, he also causes others not to covet them.
The King said, "I pray that you, O Benevolent One, will have compassion for me and walk upon my clothes, so that I may obtain immeasurable merit throughout the long night."
Sudāsa spoke according to the king's intention and stepped upon the robe.
The king said, "This robe already belongs to Sudāsa; where shall I place it?"
Sudra replied, "Great King!
You should look throughout this kingdom for those whose bodies are exposed and uncovered, and you may give your garments to them."

The king immediately commanded his attendants to take this robe out and bestow it upon the poor. When the poor people together received the king’s fine silk robe, they were all filled with joy and thought of Sudāna:
"How shall we repay his kindness and Sudāna's sincere intention?"
Through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, a voice arose from mid-air and spoke these verses:
"Not with incense, flowers, or jewels, Nor with sweet and delicious foods, Can one repay this compassionate kindness;
One must simply give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment."
"The Perfected One does not covet nobility, nor does he delight in various wonders;
to repay [his kindness], one should seek the Buddha and the mind of the four immeasurables of the Mahāyāna.

Thereupon, on the day of the full moon, Sūrata, together with the great multitude, and the King, along with all the members of his harem and the officials and commoners, went together to visit the Buddha.

At that time, ten billion laymen and laywomen of Śrāvastī, along with the poor who had been granted colorful robes, heard that Sūrata was about to go to the place where the Buddha was, and they all followed him.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, descended from the city of Śrāvastī to the Jeta Grove. Along the way, he manifested a great palace like the celestial palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and created trees made of the seven precious jewels. Beneath these trees, he prepared lion thrones for the Buddha, square and circular in proportion, and spread various kinds of silken fabrics upon them. He then stationed twelve thousand dancing girls in rows around them, performing a hundred kinds of music as an offering to the Buddha.
The Buddha, knowing that the great assembly had arrived, immediately rose and proceeded to the Great Hall, where he sat upon the celestial lion throne.
From his body, the Buddha emitted a brilliant light that illuminated heaven and earth, while flowers were scattered from the air, falling like rain.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to his son:
"Kauśika! I have prepared a seat for the Buddha; you may prepare seats for the various bodhisattvas and true persons."
The Prince immediately manifested more than sixty thousand seats, all exquisitely adorned, and spread upon them five-colored celestial woolen cloths. He then spoke these verses:
“O True Persons and Bodhisattvas, I pray you come and sit upon these seats.
These are manifestations for the delight of devas; May we always aspire to assemble before the Buddha.”

When the bodhisattvas and great disciples had taken their seats, the deva Pañcaśikha commanded his celestial attendants to tune more than five hundred lutes, ensuring the tones were harmonious as they proceeded to sing.
“The Buddha has sent Sūrata; he must surely be accompanied by powerful devas as his leaders, so we must retreat.
Thereupon, they composed verses to harmonize their minds, saying:
“His wisdom and conduct transcend a hundred kalpas; With abundant wisdom, he bestows immeasurable gifts.”
With wisdom and precepts restraining body and speech, one should pay homage to the Unsurpassed Sage.
With patience that commits no offense, with diligence and human strength,
and opening the gates of benevolence, concentration, and wisdom— one should pay homage to the Hero of the Three Realms.
Having clearly severed lust, anger, and delusion, and having exhausted them so that they are extinguished and without flaw, he has attained this for himself and bestows it upon others;
one should pay homage to the Teacher of Gods and Humans.
Through wise observation, he has eliminated the three cravings and does not covet worldly glory.
Serene and indifferent, free from sorrow and fear, one should pay homage to this Dharma King.
When Māra sent forth his three daughters, his resolve for the Way remained unshaken;
being without attachment, he could not be defiled—this most pure one, one should pay homage to.
With the thirty-two extraordinary marks, his body is adorned with the various secondary signs;
his eightfold voice reaches everywhere—homage should be paid to the God among Gods.
As he walks the earth, the wheel-mark appears upon his feet; his fearlessness and majesty resound afar.
With even teeth and shoulders rounded, you are the deity among Śākyas; I should pay homage to you.
I praise the King of Ten Powers, whose singular joy is sincerity;
by taking refuge in the Buddha, one gains merit—may I later become like the World-Honored One.

At that time, Sūrata, together with the great assembly of people and several thousand devas and humans, went to where the Buddha was. They all prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and each sat to one side.
King Prasenajit, together with his retinue, went forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
Thereupon, the king took a seat with his own hands and said to Sūrata,
"I pray that you, O Virtuous One, will sit upon this seat."
Among the assembly of devas, those who had not yet seen Sudāna thought:
"What merit does this poor man possess that he is thus honored?
Śakra, knowing the thoughts of the devas, said:
“Those who rely on merit should not disparage such a person.
Why is this? I can bear witness:
the way this person guards the precepts and honors the Dharma is beyond compare; wait but a moment, and you shall behold their virtue.”
Sudāna, wishing to cause the minds of the devas to be resolved, addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain how a bodhisattva attains majestic spiritual power and receives veneration, until reaching the path of unsurpassed, right, and true enlightenment."

At that time, the Buddha emitted a radiance from his body that blazed upon Sūrata; its form surpassed that of Śakra, Lord of Devas, by a hundred thousandfold. The deities were all delighted and, knowing he was no ordinary man, they all scattered celestial flowers upon him.
The Buddha told Sūrata:
"When a bodhisattva is noble, he does not become arrogant; when he manifests as lowly or base, he can cause people to neither crave wealth and status nor resent poverty. This is pure virtue."

When one among the wealthy and noble is able to lead others to give rise to the intention of practicing generosity; when one who possesses wisdom manifests as ignorant and is thus able to cause the foolish to quickly understand wisdom—this is called pure virtue.

Having already been able to control the mind, as you, Sūrata, have demonstrated by appearing in extreme poverty yet maintaining the precepts according to the Dharma, you are revered by the assembly of brahmins and householders; this is what is called pure knowledge of skillful means.
The venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"How long has it been since Sūrata began his training?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"He has studied for a very long time and has already served several hundred thousand billion Buddhas; he has presently attained the three patiences and mastered manifold wisdoms. He practices all forms of goodness and, seeing his own poverty and lowliness, his mind is thus purified."
Ānanda said,
"Is there now anyone who aspires to seek Buddhahood?
The Buddha said:

"Seven thousand gods of the desire realm, twelve thousand gods of the form realm, and several thousand people of the human world all gave rise to the aspiration for supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment.
Ānanda asked again:
"How long will it be before Sūrata shall become a Buddha?"
"What is the name of that Buddha,
and what is the nature of his land?
The Buddha spoke these verses for Ānanda:
“Ānanda, listen as I speak of the original aspiration of Sulabha:
protecting people without enmity and being virtuous, his merit was vast and his giving ever great;
from the time he first conceived this intention until now, its number is difficult to recount in detail.”
Making offerings to the Buddha without weariness, Revering the Dharma and guarding it without forgetfulness,
Training in the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā), Advancing on the Path with joy for a long duration,
The pure conduct (brahmacarya) never leaking away, Guarding the Dharma and wisdom so they do not falter.
Complete in conduct and resolve, he stands awakened upon the stages of the Path.
Having crossed over the net of all evils, his nature is virtuous and he awakens to internal matters.
He has already abandoned the eight worldly concerns: gain and loss, defamation and praise.
Behold all with an equal mind, Like space, free from obstruction.
Love the Dharma and practice without weariness; Make patience and compassion your constant guide.
Love others as you love yourself; Sacrifice your own body to bring peace to all beings.
He fully instructs them in the habituation of love; with mature mindfulness, he explains the reality of the meaning.
His awakened mind never departs from the Dharma; understanding emptiness, he leads others to the two liberations.
Possessing the three patiences and being free from discursive thought, he studies the Dharma and knows what should be practiced.
Wherever he went, he invariably provided guidance, and all were graced by his benevolence.
In whatever kingdoms or towns he arose, he would immediately travel to those regions to proclaim the teachings according to the Buddha’s intent, instructing all devas and humans everywhere.
After my parinirvāṇa, at the end of this final age,
Sulabha shall pass away and be reborn in the eastern land of Abhirati, in the region of Akṣobhya’s mountain.
For another three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he shall fulfill his practices and accomplish his great vows.
Having attained Buddhahood, he eliminates the world's perversities and brings peace and security as he delivers beings throughout the ten directions;
naturally becoming a divine general, he is titled the World-Honored King.
From the beginning, like Akṣobhya Buddha, those delivered by him are immeasurable.
In that world, fame and virtue will flourish; evil shall be extinguished and the righteous dharma shall arise.
The Buddha shall remain for ten million years, and the Sangha shall be beyond measure.
Arhats shall be few, while those who seek Buddhahood shall be exceedingly numerous.
At that time, human power and spiritual feet, diligence, meritorious conduct, and clarity—
within the world of the five musical tones, the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma is heard everywhere;
there is no evil Māra who can destroy goodness, and through right faith, one is liberated from the afflictions of the heterodox.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, eighty-four thousand people will uphold the sublime Dharma and illuminate the world;
they will practice the intent of non-contention as taught by Sūrata, and many will aspire to the Mahāyāna.
"All shall be born in that world; there is no counting those already delivered.
The Buddha paid homage to Sūrata.

At that time, the devas, humans, ghosts, and nāgas seated in the assembly each offered fine robes to Sūrata; the sound of their joyful acclaim was heard throughout the trichiliocosm, and hundreds of thousands of millions of people all came to pay him reverence.
The Buddha extensively expounded for him various essential teachings to explain the practices of the Three Vehicles.
King Prasenajit withdrew from his seat, joined his palms in reverence, and stood before the Buddha, saying:

"I was intoxicated by the wealth of my kingdom through greed and corruption; arrogant and self-indulgent, I engaged in perilous conduct. Only upon hearing the wondrous words of Susīma did I realize that I am the most impoverished of all."

Now I wish to renounce my home and kingdom to entrust them to the crown prince, and to receive the precepts of the World-Honored One, becoming a bhikṣu in the Buddha’s saṃgha to serve as a gardener and attendant.
I shall divide my current wealth and treasures into three parts:
one part I offer to the disciples of the Buddha; [the other two parts are for my parents and myself].
One portion shall be bestowed upon the people of the kingdom;
three portions shall be retained as official reserves.

Having received the grace of the Buddha, I shall no longer take pleasure in the wealth and treasures manifest in this life; all such blessings shall be given to sentient beings, and I vow to attain the aspiration for supreme, true, and correct enlightenment.

At that time, five hundred elders and householders, five hundred brahmins, and five hundred minor officials sitting in the assembly, having heard the King’s vow which was like the roar of a lion, all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path. They all renounced desire and, with faith in the household life, left home to practice the Way and sought to become śramaṇas; except for three hundred people among them, the Buddha ordained all the rest as śramaṇas.
Thereupon, Sūrata withdrew to sit at the side, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I also wish to follow the Holy Lion and the Buddhas currently residing throughout the ten directions, seeking their compassion to become a śramaṇa; may my wisdom and power be as those achieved by the Tathāgata."
He then entered into samādhi, and all the Buddhas currently residing throughout the ten directions appeared together with their assemblies of bhikṣus.
Sudarśana immediately rose, prostrated himself before the Buddhas of the ten directions, and became a śramaṇa. He further entreated them, saying:
"I pray that the World-Honored Ones will compassionately grant me their acceptance so that I may attain establishment."
The Buddhas of the ten directions and Śākyamuni all extended their right arms and stroked Sūrata’s head; the arms of each Buddha appeared distinctly without obstructing one another.

At that time, light illuminated the trichiliocosm, and the heavens rained down various flowers. The worthy Sūrata was naturally clothed in the Dharma-robe, his garments perfectly adjusted and his deportment serene and composed.

When Susthita had prostrated himself, five hundred bhikṣus attained the exhaustion of outflows and liberation of mind, with all fetters and bonds severed; one thousand bodhisattvas attained the stage of patient acceptance (*kṣānti*).
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Receive this prediction and this prostration-sūtra, uphold it, and you shall expound its meaning for the sake of the multitude."

Why is this? Because most people in the world of the final age are caught in the net of false faith; for this reason, I manifest as a Buddha therein to transform their evil intentions and lead them to see the Right Path, so that they may follow the example of Sūrata, entering into wisdom through faith.
I have preached the Dharma throughout the world; until even a single person has been delivered, I shall never abandon it.

Therefore, Ānanda, you must transmit this Dharma so that people may believe and delight in it, practicing and hearing it daily until their minds are opened and liberated; from this, they shall surely attain the essential goal.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, all were filled with joy; the bhikṣu Sūrata, the assembly of bhikṣus, Śakra Devendra, King Prasenajit, and the devas, humans, and asuras, all delighted in hearing it.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Sundarī-nanda (or Śūradatta)
